prompt: In `meet.go` the sender reached `ch <- "ping"` at 0 ms on an unbuffered channel, and the receiver arrived at 300 ms. When did the send return?
hint: An unbuffered channel has no room for the value.

choices.text: At 0 ms, leaving the value in the channel
choices.why: There is nowhere in an unbuffered channel to leave it.

choices.text: At 300 ms, when the value was taken
choices.why: Right. The send waits for the receiver; that meeting is the rendezvous.

choices.text: Never: the program deadlocked
choices.why: The receiver did come, so both moved on at 300 ms.

choices.text: At 600 ms, after a second round trip
choices.why: There is one crossing and no acknowledgement travelling back.

prompt: In the run of `meet.go`, `receiver: got ping` printed before `sender: the send returned`, both at 300ms. On another run, may the two lines swap?
hint: What is promised is about the value crossing, not about the next `Println`.

choices.text: Yes: after the handoff the two are independent again
choices.why: Right. Each line only waits for the crossing, not for the other goroutine's print.

choices.text: No: the receiver's line always comes first
choices.why: Nothing orders the two prints after the crossing.

choices.text: No: the sender's line always comes first, as it sent first
choices.why: In the captured run it came second, which already rules this out.

choices.text: Only with the race detector on
choices.why: There is no race here; the order of two independent prints is simply open.

prompt: A worker sends `"done"` on an unbuffered channel when it finishes. When the send returns, what does the worker know that it would not know with a buffered channel?
hint: Section 03 lists what a buffer removes.

choices.text: That the channel has been closed
choices.why: Nothing about a send says anything about a close.

choices.text: That no other goroutine is running
choices.why: Other goroutines may run freely; the send concerns two of them.

choices.text: That a receiver has taken the message
choices.why: Right. A buffered send that returns only says the value is in the buffer.

choices.text: That the receiver has finished handling the message
choices.why: It knows the value was received, not what the receiver did with it afterwards.

prompt: `buffered.go` sent into `make(chan int, 3)` with nobody receiving until 300 ms. How many sends returned at 0 ms?
hint: As many as the buffer holds.

prompt: In `buffered.go` the fourth send returned at 300 ms. What freed it?
hint: Look at the line printed just before it.

choices.text: The buffer grew to hold four
choices.why: A channel's capacity is fixed when it is made; `cap` printed 3 throughout.

choices.text: The receiver took `1`, freeing a slot
choices.why: Right: `received 1` at 300 ms, then `sent 4` at once, with `len` back at 3.

choices.text: The sender's goroutine was preempted after 300 ms
choices.why: Preemption hands over a processor; it cannot make room in a channel.

choices.text: The `close(ch)` at the end of the loop
choices.why: The close comes after the fifth send, and a close never frees room.

prompt: A producer makes 1,000 items a second and the consumer handles 800. Someone raises the buffer from 100 to 10,000. What happens?
hint: A buffer absorbs a burst; what about a difference that lasts?

choices.text: The consumer speeds up to keep the buffer from filling
choices.why: A buffer changes nothing about how fast the consumer works.

choices.text: The mismatch is gone, since the buffer is now large enough
choices.why: 200 items a second pile up whatever the size; a larger buffer only fills later.

choices.text: It fills later, at about 50 s, and then sends block again
choices.why: Right. The surplus of 200 a second fills 10,000 slots in 50 s; then sends block, as before.

choices.text: The program deadlocks when the buffer fills
choices.why: The consumer is still receiving, so a full buffer slows the producer rather than stopping everything.

prompt: Match each channel state with what a send does in it.
hint: Only room decides, unless nobody has room for it.

prompt: `stuck.go` ended with `goroutine 1 [chan send]`. What does the bracketed part tell you?
hint: Each goroutine in a deadlock report carries one.

choices.text: The type of the channel involved
choices.why: The type was `chan int`; the brackets say what the goroutine was doing.

choices.text: How long the goroutine had been blocked
choices.why: A duration appears in some reports, but `chan send` is an operation, not a time.

choices.text: That the channel had been closed
choices.why: Sending on a closed channel panics with its own message. This one was open.

choices.text: What it was waiting to do: send on a channel
choices.why: Right, at line 8, `ch <- 42`.

prompt: Changing `make(chan int)` to `make(chan int, 1)` made `stuck.go` print 42. A colleague concludes buffered channels cannot deadlock. What is wrong with that?
hint: What if the program sent two values before receiving?

choices.text: Nothing: a buffer removes the need for a receiver
choices.why: It removes it only until the buffer is full.

choices.text: A second send before the receive would block
choices.why: Right. A buffer moves the point where a program deadlocks; it does not decide whether it does.

choices.text: Buffered channels deadlock more often than unbuffered ones
choices.why: The lesson makes no such comparison; the size only moves where blocking starts.

choices.text: `go vet` would have flagged the buffered version
choices.why: `go vet` passed the unbuffered one too; it cannot see this.

prompt: `partial.go` left a goroutine stuck on a send for its whole run, yet it exited with status 0 and no error. Why did the runtime say nothing?
hint: When exactly does the deadlock check fire?

choices.text: The goroutine was not counted by `NumGoroutine`
choices.why: It was: the count was 2 each time.

choices.text: A send inside a goroutine is never checked
choices.why: The check is about all goroutines together, wherever the send is.

choices.text: `main` was asleep, not blocked
choices.why: Right. The check fires only when every goroutine is blocked.

choices.text: The comment on the send told the compiler to ignore it
choices.why: Comments mean nothing to the compiler or the runtime.

prompt: When every goroutine in a program is blocked, the runtime stops it with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - ___!`
hint: The word the lesson is named after.

prompt: `partial.go` printed `goroutines alive: 2` three times. How many of those two goroutines were stuck for good?
Put the lines of the `buffered.go` run in the order they were printed.
hint: Three sends first, then the receiver frees one slot at a time.

prompt: A handler starts a goroutine that sends its result on `ch := make(chan Result)`, then returns early on an error without receiving. The server runs for weeks. What happens on each such error?
hint: This is `partial.go` inside a program that never ends.

choices.text: The runtime reports a deadlock on the first one
choices.why: Other goroutines are alive and serving, so the check never fires.

choices.text: The send panics once the handler has returned
choices.why: Nothing closes the channel; the send simply waits.

choices.text: The goroutine is collected when the handler returns
choices.why: A blocked goroutine is never collected; it holds its stack and everything it refers to.

choices.text: One more goroutine stays stuck, silently, and memory grows
choices.why: Right. A leak, lesson 6's subject; a buffer of one would let that send complete.

prompt: What do `len(ch)` and `cap(ch)` report for a buffered channel?

choices.text: Values sent so far, and values received so far
choices.why: Neither counts history. `buffered.go` sent five, and `len` never passed 3.

choices.text: Values waiting in the buffer, and its size
choices.why: Right. `cap` is fixed when the channel is made; `len` moves as values go in and out.

choices.text: Goroutines waiting to send, and goroutines waiting to receive
choices.why: Neither counts goroutines; `runtime.NumGoroutine` does that, for the whole program.

choices.text: The size of one element in bytes, and the buffer's size in bytes
choices.why: Both count values, not bytes.

prompt: For the 300 ms that `meet.go`'s sender waited on its send, what was its goroutine doing?

choices.text: Checking the channel in a loop, using a processor
choices.why: A blocked send does not spin; the scheduler parks the goroutine.

choices.text: Holding the channel locked so the receiver could not use it
choices.why: The receiver used it the moment it arrived.

choices.text: Nothing: it was parked, using no processor
choices.why: Right, exactly like a goroutine in `time.Sleep`.

choices.text: Copying the value into a buffer the runtime made for it
choices.why: An unbuffered channel gets no hidden buffer; the value crosses at the meeting.

prompt: Two goroutines each send on an unbuffered channel the other one is supposed to receive from, and each sends before it receives. Nothing else runs. What happens?
hint: Each send waits for a receiver that is itself waiting to send.

choices.text: One of the two wins and the other follows
choices.why: Neither can win: each send needs the other goroutine to be at its receive, and neither ever gets there.

choices.text: A fatal deadlock error, if `main` is blocked too
choices.why: Right. Both are in `[chan send]`; if nothing else can move, the runtime stops the program.

choices.text: The values cross in both directions at once
choices.why: A send and a receive must meet on the same channel; two sends do not meet each other.

choices.text: A panic: send on a channel with no receiver
choices.why: There is no such panic; a send without a receiver waits.
